paras: The Cooper whippings were floggings of Black men at Cooper, Delta County, Texas, in June 1903, after which the men were driven from the county. According to a Dallas dispatch, three Black "leaders" were taken from their homes and flogged on a Wednesday night, three others had been whipped a week earlier, and notices posted around the town warned Black residents to leave. Papers carried two differing accounts, one calling the victims criminals, the other tying the floggings to criticism of a Black man's prison sentence.

About two weeks before the floggings, a Black man named Walker had received a life sentence for "attempting to assault a white woman." The men later whipped were "charged with having made insolent criticism" of that trial and sentence. A Spanish-language account in La Correspondencia de Puerto Rico rendered their offence as having complained that the sentenced man had not had the full protection of the law.

For about a week before June 26, notices posted "in conspicuous places" warned Black residents to leave Cooper "or take the consequences." About a week before the main flogging, three Black men had been whipped. Then, on the night of Wednesday, apparently June 24, three men described as "negro leaders" were taken from their homes and "severely flogged." The flogged men were "compelled to leave the county," and the dispatch named neither them nor their attackers.

A New Orleans dispatch of the same date told it differently: "the Regulars" had taken out the town's "negro loafers, negro sneak thieves and petty criminals," whipped them and ordered them to leave town. In this version, the excitement over the whipping was followed by placards ordering "some of the better class negroes" to leave.

The placarded Black residents complained to the authorities, and white and Black citizens then met, at the court house according to the New Orleans dispatch and on Thursday night according to the Dallas one. In the New Orleans telling, the whites pledged support to "all orderly negroes," who promised in turn to help keep down the lawless element and report lawbreakers to the authorities. In the Dallas telling, the well-behaved could stay, but "the worthless, insolent and dangerous negroes would have to go."

According to the New Orleans dispatch, an investigation found that the warnings on the houses had been placed there by "mischievous boys." The Dallas dispatch reported that officers were searching for the men who did the flogging, but no report of arrests, an indictment or a trial appears in the coverage.

The New York Sun printed the New Orleans dispatch on June 27 as "Bad Negroes Coming North," presenting Cooper as starting in Texas a movement, begun in Ellisville and Laurel, Mississippi, to "unload" Black criminals on the North. The same day the Minneapolis Journal objected editorially to Southern towns unloading disorderly Black people on the North, yet found it "reassuring" that orderly Black residents of Cooper had been promised protection. The same New Orleans text ran in South Carolina in the Yorkville Enquirer on July 1 and, credited to the Sun, in the Anderson Intelligencer and the Keowee Courier on July 8.

The Dallas account appeared in the Corvallis Times on July 1 and in the Mexico (Missouri) Message on July 2 as "Insolent Negroes Given a Flogging." La Correspondencia de Puerto Rico took a different line under the heading "El problema racista en los Estados Unidos," saying the men had been beaten "inhumanamente" and setting the episode beside more than ten lynchings in two weeks and Black plans to emigrate to Liberia. All of the coverage found appeared in white papers; none was found in the Black press or in Texas newspapers.

The two dispatches disagree on who was whipped and why: the New Orleans account called the victims loafers, sneak thieves and petty criminals taken out by "the Regulars," while the Dallas account called them "negro leaders" punished for criticizing the Walker sentence. They also differ on the notices: a week-long warning before the floggings in the Dallas dispatch, placards left by boys after the whipping in the New Orleans one. The Texas-datelined Dallas version is the more specific, giving the number of victims, the night and the charge.

reader.title: Cooper whippings
bases: Unidentified men posted notices warning Black residents to leave Cooper, took Black men from their homes at night, flogged them and compelled them to leave the county (A3, A5), and one dispatch attributes the whippings to 'the Regulars' (A1).

accounts.label: Dallas dispatch
accounts.gist: After a week of notices warning Black residents to leave Cooper, three 'negro leaders' were taken from their homes and flogged on Wednesday night, three others had been whipped a week before, and all were made to leave the county for criticizing the Walker sentence; officers were hunting the floggers.

accounts.label: New Orleans dispatch
accounts.gist: 'The Regulars' whipped Cooper's 'negro loafers, negro sneak thieves and petty criminals' and ordered them out; placards later put on better-class Black homes were found to be the work of boys.

accounts.label: Puerto Rican correspondent
accounts.gist: Paraphrasing the Dallas account, said the men were beaten 'inhumanamente' and fled the county, their only offence having been to complain that another Black man had not had the full protection of the law.

framing.detail: The Sun's 'Bad Negroes Coming North' / 'Southern Cities Driving Out the Loafers and Criminals' presented the whippings as part of a movement to rid the South of 'the disorderly negro element'.
The Minneapolis Journal objected to criminals being unloaded on the North but called it 'reassuring' that orderly Black residents of Cooper were promised protection.
The Mexico Message headlined 'Insolent Negroes Given a Flogging' and 'Citizens Warn Worthless Blacks to Leave Cooper, Texas', while reporting that officers sought the floggers.
The Corvallis Times ran the Dallas dispatch without headline in a news-briefs column.

La Correspondencia de Puerto Rico, under 'El problema racista en los Estados Unidos', said the men were beaten 'inhumanamente' for a trivial offence and set the episode beside a count of more than ten lynchings in two weeks.

versions.value: Three 'negro leaders' flogged Wednesday night and three others a week earlier, charged with 'insolent criticism' of the Walker trial and sentence.
'Negro loafers, negro sneak thieves and petty criminals' taken out by 'the Regulars', whipped and ordered to leave town.

conflicts.note: The Dallas version is more specific (numbers, the night, the stated offence, the officers' search) and its Texas dateline is nearer the scene; the New Orleans version folds Cooper into a general regional story about driving out criminals.

versions.value: Notices posted for a week before the floggings in conspicuous places warning Black residents to leave Cooper or take the consequences.
Placards on houses of 'better class' Black residents appeared after the whipping and an investigation found they were put there by 'mischievous boys'.

conflicts.note: The finding about boys comes from an unnamed investigation reported only in the New Orleans dispatch.
